speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as supply for this year will have become exhausted on March 31 and we do not reassemble until April 9, the public service would be seriously hampered and the public interest would be detrimentally affected if we did not pass interim supply. Of course, I can proceed only by unanimous consent but I ask the house for unanimous consent for the passing of interim supply of one-sixth of the main estimates for next year. I am asking for one-sixth rather than one-twelfth because under the new act we require a larger proportion than was the case under the old practice. I can go into further details if the house so desires. To-day being Thursday, when the motion to go into supply is put, Mr. Speaker leaves the chair without question put, but inasmuch as I am asking for unanimous consent I suppose I would have to make a motion, which I now make.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL

speechtext:
I should like
to take advantage of this opportunity, which is the first I have had since seeing the auditor general's report for the year ending March 31, 1933, to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance, of the Prime Minister, and in fact of parliament, to a statement which appears in that report and which is of very grave concern, I think, to hon. members of this house and to parliament itself. The statement appears on page 55 of the introduction under the head, " Operation of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act." The auditor general there states:
As tlie present report is the first one covering a full year's operation under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act of 1931, [_ consider that I should state, for the informa-lion of parliament, how this act, amending as it does the previous act, has altered the duties and modified the responsibilities of the auditor general acting as an officer of parliament, and the resultant effect on parliamentary control of expenditure of public moneys.
I need not complete that paragraph. The next one reads:
There is, however, another aspect of the changes made by the new act which calls for special consideration at this time as it involves the principle of parliamentary control over the Issue of public moneys. Under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act of 1878, provision was uade for the appointment of an officer who ,vould be independent of the government of the day and be answerable to parliament alone in respect of such issues. However, under the Amending Act of 1931, the power of issue of appropriated moneys was removed from that officer, the auditor general, whose powers are now restricted to the examination of accounts and the reporting thereon to parliament. The cases cited hereunder may indicate an inclination to overlook the statutory limitations regarding the expenditure of moneys appropriated, thereby diminishing parliamentary control of these moneys. Under the old act, if the auditor general objected to certain expenditures on the ground that they were not properly authorized, he could refuse to make further issues of moneys; but under the new act he has no such power.
On the next page the auditor general gives instances of the result of the withdrawal of his control over the issue of public moneys.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext:
Perhaps the right hon.
gentleman would not mind reading those.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext:
I shall be
glad to read them. I had intended doing so. The point Ito which I wish to direct the attention of the house is that, by the Audit Act of 1931, the control which formerly this parliament had over public expenditures, by having its servant, the auditor general, made responsible for the issuing of appropriated moneys, has apparently been withdrawn; that power which the auditor general formerly had
has been withdrawn and vested in an officer who is not a servant of parliament but an official of the government, one whom the government has it in its power to dismiss. Let me say at once that I have the highest appreciation of the worth of the present official, and I do not for one moment assume that there will be in his case any possibility of action of that kind. But I do think it is most important that parliament should retain the power, which it has had for fifty years, of exercising control over public expenditures in the manner in which formerly it did. I submit that at the time the bill was introduced the house was not given to understand -that the new appointment of comptroller provided by the act meant any withdrawal from the auditor general of this particular function, which is the most important of all he formerly had, and placing it in the hands of an officer of one of the departments of government. Had the house so understood, I am sure there would have been strong opposition to such a proposal, and that the house would never have consented thereto. I am not sure that when the government brought in the bill its members appreciated the fact that this would be the consequence. The Prime Minister has asked me to read what the auditor says with regard to the Sffect of the change. I will do so. On page 5G of the introduction he states:
Availability of one vote to cover overexpenditure under another. On pages 195 and 198 of this volume is printed the correspondence with the comptroller of the treasury and the treasury board relative to the procedure followed in the case of several departments which in my opinion was subversive of the principle of parliamentary control over the expenditure of public monej's. In each case the over-expenditure on one vote was charged against a surplus on a vote provided for another purpose. Under section 27 (1) of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act it is provided that all issues of public moneys shall be made under the direction and control of the comptroller but no such issue shall be made in excess of any appropriation. Under section 50 (2) I am obliged to call the attention of the House of Commons to every case in which a grant has been exceeded. The only definite prohibitive direction to the comptroller in the act is that he shall not issue any money in excess of a parliamentary appropriation, and the first duty laid upon me in respect of my report to the House of Commons is that I shall call attention to every case where that prohibition has not been observed. These statutory directions are valueless if the procedure followed in these three cases is to become the accepted practice. Such practice is contrary to the underlying principle of supplementary estimates and of the issue of governor general's warrants. In confirmation of my views I cited previous treasury board decisions, resolutions of the British House of Commons and the debate in our House of
Supply Bill-Mr. Rhodes

Commons in 1888 between leaders on both sides relative to this subject. The principle of parliamentary control is so fundamentally important that I feel impelled to call attention to any departure therefrom.
Payment from general vote of gratuities in lieu of retiring leave.-In volume 1 of my report for 1931-32 (page 286) and page 187 of this volume is printed correspondence with the treasury board in reference to the payment of gratuities in lieu of retiring leave without any special vote having been provided by parliament. In my opinion this was irregular ^ in that payments were made as gratuities, equivalent to or less than the retiring leave authorized by statute, from votes provided by parliament for other purposes. The treasury board differed from this view.
Since then another order in council has been passed, dated' July 31, 1933. providing for the retirement of employees who have reached a certain age limit, with gratuities equivalent to retiring leave of so many months' salary. In some of these cases the gratuities were in excess of the retiring leave that may be granted under the Civil Service Act, and in other cases gratuities were paid to employees who are entitled to no retiring leave under any act of parliament. No special vote was provided and the payments have been charged to various votes under the respective departments. Although the present retirements are being effected in the interest of good administration a procedure is established under which, without any authority other than that provided in an order in council and without any special appropriation being provided, gratuities are being paid to retired employees in excess of those payable under the Civil Service Act, or are not authorized by any statute. The question of the advisability of obtaining a vote of parliament to cover such expenditures has been resubmitted recently for the consideration of the treasury board. The British practice in cases of this kind is determined by a decision of the treasury in the following terms: "My Lords fully agree with the view of the committee that if in exceptional circumstances a gratuity is given on retirement in addition to the statutory superannuation payments, that gratuity should not be paid until an estimate making clear its extrastatutory nature has been presented to parliament and passed."
I shall now read the concluding paragraph:
Howrever I have certified all applications submitted to me for pre-audit as this question had been dealt with in my previous annual report but I feel that the matter should again be brought to the attention of the House of Commons since this class of payments has been extended to cover gratuities that are in excess of what is provided by the Civil Service Act.
The auditor general in the report states in so many words that the Civil Service Act has been violated; that moneys which were voted for one purpose, have been used for another; that moneys have been paid out of the public treasury without any previous appropriation by parliament for the specific purpose and that these violations of a former practice have grown out of the fact that by

the Audit Act of 1931 there was taken away from the auditor general as the servant of this parliament the power which he had for many years exercised of issue of appropriated moneys to be placed to the credit of the different government departments. Certainly the house was given to understand that the purpose of the Audit Act was to bring about a more effective control and not to lessen it; least of all was it thought that its purpose was to transfer control which parliament has most zealously exercised from the very beginning, to the government and to an officer under the government's control. When I read this statement in the auditor general's report I felt it iny duty to bring the matter immediately to the attention of the house, not with a desire of provoking a discussion on the question, but with a view of seeing once this had been done whether in the mind of the government the Audit Act should not be amended so that parliament may have restored to it that power over expenditure of public moneys through the control of issue of appropriated moneys by its servant the auditor general, which has been customary ever since the first audit act was passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: So far as the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act is concerned, the question of parliamentary control, I submit with all deference, does not arise. All the auditor general is doing in that statement is calling in question an action of parliament itself. Parliament may or may not have acted wisely in passing that act. It may be a question whether there is or is not that same degree of control which obtained under the previous method. But inasmuch as I did not know my right hon. friend intended to bring this matter up to-day and also in view of the circumstance that I have asked unanimous consent of the house, I would be the last to wish to consume time under those conditions. I take it that the purposes of my right hon. friend will have been met if I say to him that I shall be very glad to take his references to-day as a notice and to indicate to him that I shall be pleased indeed at a later stage in supply or at some time when it may be convenient other than when we are voting interim supply, to discuss the question in full detail.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: I would certainly have given my hon. friend notice of what I intended to say-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am not criticizing my
hon. friend for not doing so.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext:
-had I meant in any way to start a discussion. In reading the report I noticed the statement by the auditor

Supply Bill-Mr. Bennett
general and as I believed it was of concern to parliament I considered it my duty to bring it immediately to the attention of the house. I thank my hon. friend for promising to give it consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext:
I saw the volume of the auditor general's report to which reference has been made, and while I did not read the details of the matter, because I was familiar with the position taken by the auditor general, I at once recognized the references when the right hon. gentleman read them. The truth is that the new act entirely changed the conditions under which moneys were made available for departmental expenditures. The truth is also that the auditor general has always disapproved of it. It wiped out the entire bookkeeping establishments in the several departments and instead of credits being granted by the auditor general, they are now referable to the votes of parliament under the comptroller and unless there is provision in the estimate of the particular department for the payment of the moneys that are sought to be expended, then the auditor general declines to sanction the payment when the item comes before him. I do not propose to do more than to say that the effect of the action taken has been to save the country, I think the figure for last year was $231,000-I speak subject to correction-because the new method is partly responsible for the reduction in personnel mentioned in the return made a few days ago by the Minister of Finance. I feel satisfied that when the right hon. gentleman and those associated with him have studied the operations of the act, they will be satisfied that parliamentary control has not been lessened and that the machinery set up for handling the financial operations of the country is such as would obtain in good business establishments and retain to the utmost the control of parliament.
I said to my colleague the Minister of Finance that in view of the attention of the house having been directed to the matter by the right hon. gentleman, we might discuss it fully when the house is again in supply on Monday or Tuesday or any other day that might be convenient. Possibly the best time would be when the item of cost of management in connection with the financial operations of the country is under consideration by the committee. Every facility that can be afforded for the purpose of the discussion will be given and if the right hon. gentleman will indicate that there is any information he desires to be furnished from the department, I will see that it is made available for him before the discussion takes place.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: In connection with the Prime Minister's promise a few minutes ago to bring down information to help in understanding the matter of control of public expenditure, perhaps he or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) will be kind enough to have the officers of the department prepare a memorandum which will show by comparison the old system of control and the new and what the differences between the two may be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: Yes, certainly, that will be done.

subtopic: VOTE OF ONE-SIXTH OF ESTIMATES FOR FINANCIAL
speechtext: I think I am correct in saying that the amount which it is now proposed to vote, is not for March salaries or for payments due to the public to March 31 of this year, but it is intended to cover moneys which will be due to civil servants and to other people who are doing business with the government for the months of April and May. Before the vote is carried, I think this is a very opportune time for the government to tell the house whether we are going to return to the payment of 100 per cent of salaries to lighthouse keepers, customs officials and other officers of the service throughout the country. We should therefore have an expression of opinion from the government with regard to getting back to the payment of 100 per cent of the salaries, whether it be the salary of Mr. Speaker, or that of the Deputy Speaker of this house, or of the chairman of the committee of the whole, or my remuneration as the member for Antigonish-Guysborough, or the salaries of the deputy ministers of the different departments and other officials, or of the lightkeepers and charwomen and elevator men and all the other civil servants of this country. We should have a statement from the government now, because if we vote this money to-day and adjourn over Easter and do not come back until the 9th of April there will be very little time between then and the 15th when the cheques go out for the government to take any action. This vote, as the finance minister said in answer to my question, only covers the amount set forth in the estimates, and as we know, in these estimates the ten per cent is deducted. It is very easy for the finance minister and the government to bring down a supplementary estimate covering the ten per cent, the difference between 90 and 100 per cent, so that the civil servants after the first of April can get 100 per cent which in my opinion is due them.

speechtext:
The fact remains that unemployment relief has been the child of the federal government since the fall of 1930. That policy was inaugurated then by this government and has been administered by the provincial authorities. Another feature of this is the fact that for the first year, 1930-31, the government had a public works policy, but for reasons known only to them, it was found wanting and abrogated and then they took up direct relief. That, however, does not conflict with the statement I made a few minutes ago that the provincial authorities of Ontario fully realize that direct relief is only a palliative; that it is not a remedy for the present situation, and I believe I am absolutely in order in saying that the introduction of the resolution now before us brings very forcibly before the house and the country the fact that the federal government has no policy so far as unemployment is concerned. Unemployment relief, as I say, is purely and simply the infant of th,e present government. I could quote several papers which the minister knows are Conservative in their views and which certainly are not satisfied with the present method of unemployment relief. The objection is not as to the way in which it is administered, but they relaize that it is only a palliative and they feel now that after nearly four years in power the federal government should have a policy whereby it will be able to deal with such an important national problem in a way that will satisfy every section of the population. Unemployment re-

lief at the present time is purely and simply the dole and it is a system which is largely deteriorating the moral fibre of our Canadian people. All it is doing is to permit the unemployed and their families to keep body and soul together, holding no hope for the future.
In making these remarks I want to be constructive in my criticism, but I know I have the backing of members of the Ontario government. Last summer and fall and during the winter Mr. Finlayson was quite outspoken in regard to the direct relief policy inaugurated by the federal government. He said practically that it was a scheme that should not be carried on any longer. I was hoping that the government would have a policy whereby unemployment w'ould be dealt with at the root and from the proper angle. As I said, the present method is purely and simply a small stop-gap; it is only a way whereby the people keep body and soul together hoping for better times to come. When those times are going to come, they do not know, but surely the people of Ontario and of Canada generally have a right to expect to get relief and some hope from the present administration.
I know I shall have an opportunity of speaking on the back to the land movement when that estimate comes before us and at present I want to confine my remarks to directing attention to certain works that should be imdertaken in my section of the country. Last fall the people of Canada entertained high hopes for a certain length of time because they were led to believe-I do not know from what member of the present government the report came-the government was going to inaugurate a program of public works. Whether the government had in mind at the time the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway being commenced early this spring, I do not know; but if such hopes were entertained, they were badly shattered last week. So far as eastern Canada is concerned, there is no hope of relief in the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway, but there are other programs of public works of national importance that could be undertaken by the government. It was said three years ago that it was found that the cost to the government of public work construction was practically prohibitive, but surely after three years of experiment the government can find it possible to undertake works of a national character and in an economical way. Knowing the minister so well personally, I make the statement in all sincerity that I know he is not satisfied with the resolution under discussion at the present time. I know he fully realizes, because he is conversant with the

Relief Act 1934
situation that exists throughout Canada, that the settlers in my section and his own and the farmers and workingmen generally are not satisfied under the direct relief scheme as it exists at present. Newspapers in my district, including even my regional one, have been absolutely against the relief meaures we have had on the statutes of Canada for the last few years. Surely it should be possible for the government to give employment to worthy people. It is true that under the relief provisions our people have not actually suffered greatly, that they have at least been able to eat three times a day and to be clothed to some extent, but there are anomalies in the application of those regulations. There is the fact that some able-bodied men have not done a day's work ever since relief was inaugurated, also that men who were willing to work on their farms for instance could not do it because for work done on their own property they could not receive remuneration from the government. I do not know if the Minister of Labour is familiar with the fact that last summer in our section an official of the northern development branch declared in the town of Cochrane that every settler who spent his time working on his farm would receive remuneration. That declaration was received with enthusiasm by every section of the population, urban and rural. I believe it would be a proper method of administering the Relief Act in new colonization areas. But unhappily for our fine rural population that policy was not made effective. I hope the minister will use his influence during the coming summer to see that settlers who are willing to stay on their holdings and clear their land for cultivation shall receive a certain amount of compensation, comparable to what wTas paid last summer for work on colonization roads. That policy would involve no extra cost to the administration.
Another matter which I have mentioned on several occasions, which is national in its scope and in which our section is greatly interested, is the trans-Canada highway. The minister is familiar with the promises made in his riding and in mine during the last federal election that the trans-Canada highway would go through Haileybury, Cochrane and Hearst. I am sorry to say that as far as my section is concerned it has not been routed as we expected. Consequently our people were unable to get the amount of work that was provided, for instance in the Ottawa valley and around the north shore of lake Superior. The promise was made during the last election and should be fulfilled. Some people say that election promises are only to catch votes and must be forgotten after the
vote is cast, but my section of the country will not stand for that. There was a definite promise made at that time that the route of the highway was then or would soon be decided. But as far as I can see, outside of some minor work that has been done on the Ferguson highway at Englehart and Cobalt, very little work has been done towards connecting that highway with the transcontinental highway. That promise was very definite and well-understood by every section of northern Ontario. It may be that the provincial government said two or three years ago that they were not decided on the route but surely after three years of investigation the provincial government should be willing now to give a lead as far as that highway, and our section, is concerned. We believe in our section that we have been fooled on that important question. Although we realize that certain sections of northern Ontario have a right to be connected with the trans-Canada highway, I believe the promise made during the last federal election, which was a logical promise, should be implemented. We want to be connected somewhere east of lake Nipigon with the other section. But I believe our section is being entirely forgotten at present.
To show how much money has been spent on the trans-Canada highway and how much more will have to be spent I will quote a few figures given in answer to a question of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Hurtubise) as to the amounts of money expended on the trans-Canada highway in the province of Ontario for the years 1931, 1932 and 1933. The answer given was as follows:

It is easy to see that the federal government is satisfied as long as a road is constructed in the Ottawa valley and a certain amount of work done around the north shore of lake Superior, and our section absolutely forgotten. I may tell this committee that not a single inch of work has been performed wedt of Hearst and no move made in that direction. This is work of national importance. One of the finest and most rapidly growing sections of this country is being absolutely ignored, and at the same time the route by the north shore of lake Superior is by far the more expensive. Anyone familiar with the physical obstacles in that section will readily realize that it would cost millions more to route the road that way than through our section. There is still time to remedy the injustice that has been done. We still hope in our section that through the

influence of the Minister of Labour we shall receive the justice to which we are absolutely entitled. I believe the government should inaugurate a national program of colonization roads, not only for my section of the country but for the whole dominion. It is not my intention to speak at greater length, but I must repeat that under this resolution the people of Canada cannot find satisfaction for the hopes that were entertained at the beginning of the session. Some of the ministers in the Ontario legislature and of the federal government led the people to believe that a program would be inaugurated different from the one which after three years of application has been found wanting and has not proved a solution of our problems. Having given the problem of unemployment a very thorough study I believe that instead of improving conditions the present policy is aggravating them. Further than that, I know of hundreds of young people in my section of the country who are ready and willing to work on the farms. Some of them are college graduates, and they would be willing to go back to the new land if an opportunity were given to them. But that opportunity has not been offered.
Although I have many clippings before me from newspapers in my section of the country I shall read only a few comments from the Porcupine Advance, a newspaper published weekly and well known to the Minister of Labour. This newspaper may be termed a Conservative-Independent publication, and has always fought the battles of the north country with fair-mindedness. Part of an article written last autumn is as follows:
From the earliest signs of the depression The Advance has maintained that only through the providing of employment could any true help be expected. In this young country of Canada there is so much work necessary for the development of the country that it seems absurd to refuse the opportunity for having some of the needs supplied in the way of public enterprises of various kinds. This was the solution promised by Hon. R. B. Bennett's government. It was the plan adopted first by that government and there is every reason to feel that it worked out with reasonable success.

I was not satisfied when two years ago the government found it advisable to abandon the policy of public works and to adopt one of direct relief. To-day I am not satisfied in my own mind as to why that action was taken. Some people have said that the cost of the work then done proved to be prohibitive. That is easily understandable when we remember that the work done in the winters of 1930 and 1931 was done in frozen ground. I am speaking of the construction of roads, ditches and other similar works. Surely if that policy had been followed during the summer months the cost would not have been prohibitive, and to-day the government should not be groping to find its way out of the trouble with which it is now faced.
In the name of the settlers and labourers in my section of the country, and in all sincerity I make the assertion that the people do not want the dole, but that they do want a chance to work. I am an ordinary layman, so far as financial matters are concerned, but undoubtedly if the American congress had seen fit to adopt the St. Lawrence waterways project this government would have found it possible to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a national undertaking. Where would the government have found that money? I presume that the project would have cost the Canadian people at least half a billion dollars, and that money would have had to come from somewhere. But to-day the government does not find it possible to have a national program of public works whereby our people would find the employment they deserve and wish to have. If the money could have been found for proceeding with the St. Lawrence waterway scheme it should be just as possible for the government to inaugurate a policy of public works. Further than that, if to-morrow, in another war, Canada were called upon to defend her good name and ideals, even in European countries, money would be found; there is no doubt about that. Money was found, to the extent of $60,000,000, to back the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Surely in this year of grace 1934, after the government has been experimenting for the last four years on policies which even their own friends and supporters have judged to be a complete failure, the minister should have something to offer better than he is offering at the present time. May I be permitted to bring to the attention of the minister and hon. members the report of the committee on unemployment which was recently adopted by the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion. I think this was excellently put and summarizes well the objections to the present policy of Canada, if we may call it such, with regard to unemployment.

speechtext:
Yes, policy or, as
the right hon. gentleman has said,, lack of policy of the government. I read from the report:
The general tenor of the resolutions and statements before your committee clearly indicates that the members of the Canadian Legion regard the tragic consequences of unemployment as a menace to the stability of our national life. It is equally clear that they are determined to challenge any further delay in the utilization of the national resources and credit to the fullest degree, in order to remove the peril of wide-spread poverty throughout the dominion.
It is considered that general attention should be directed to the following salient features of conditions resulting from prolonged unemployment and inadequate relief measures:-
(a)	Decreasing relief benefits with increasing living costs resulting in more general malnutrition and ill-liealth in the homes of the unemployed, with consequent danger of epidemics.
(b)	Dangerous depletion without replacement of household equipment and supplies, as well as clothing, causing unsanitary conditions and inability to exercise the ordinary precautions against physical disorders and infections.
(c)	The disastrous effects of prevailing conditions on the younger generation in the undermining of morale and physical stamina.
(d)	Insecurity of tenure of homes.
(e)	The lack of measures offering any hope for the reabsorption of the unemployed into industry, the segregation and branding of those compelled to accept relief as a class apart and outcast, and the perpetuation of conditions likely to create a permanent and dependent pauper class deprived of normal economic privileges and rights.
(f)	The general indifference and ignorance shown toward the danger of submitting a large section of the population to conditions of which the foregoing are indisputable features.
(g)	The tendency of some employers to exploit the circumstances of the unemployed in offering inadequate wages for temporary employment.
(h)	The increasing determination of the unemployed to defend their homes by any available means against the social injustice of enforcing degrading and perilous poverty upon them in the midst of plenty.
It is quite obvious that one might easily spend considerable time in expounding and illustrating each of these paragraphs.
These paragraphs are in clear and concise English and I intend to let them stand just as they are. I quote:
Your committee is of the opinion that the gravity of the situation is such as to demand immediate and drastic measures of a temporary nature that the cumulative effects of prolonged unemployment may not further menace the well-being of the entire community.
It is, therefore, recommended that this dominion convention of the Canadian legion urge upon the federal and provincial governments early ameliorative action with respect to the general problem of unemployment and relief, as indicated hereunder:
(a)	The promotion of a program of necessary public works maintenance and development, of sufficient extent and character as to absorb all able-bodied unemployed persons at a scale of wages that will ensure decent living conditions;
(b)	Pending promotion of a public works program an immediate increase in the scale of relief, commensurate with increased living costs, and with uniform application in all cities, towns, and municipalities;
(c)	Free medical, surgical, dental, and optical treatment for all recipients of unemployment relief and their families;
(d)	That in the operation of wTork camps regarded as essential in connection with public works projects, a minimum wage of $1.10 per day be paid in addition to provision of food, shelter, and clothing;
(e)	That more adequate and special provision be made for the protection of unemployed single women;
Relief Act 1934

(f)	That the provincial commands be requested to urge upon their respective provincial governments the necessity of protection for all unemployed persons against evictions and loss of their homes through foreclosure or tax sales.
Had these recommendations been made by a body other than the legion it is quite possible that those advancing them would have been called agitators, boDhevists or impossible dreamers. In my humble opinion they represent a sane and safe program which ought to be taken into serious consideration by this government. I quote:
Your committee recommends that the dominion executive council be instructed to urge upon the federal government the appointment of an economic advisory council, including economists, statisticians and engineers of unquestioned integrity and ability.	It is
further proposed that such council shall function in an advisory capacity to the government, with the main object of correlating all available data and preparing, as may be warranted by the facts, an outline of a planned economy under which,-
(a)	Industry may effectively reabsorb human labour displaced by technological advancement.
(b)	A national financial policy may be so determined as to properly relate distribution to production and enable such adjustment of the monetary system as will give paramount consideration to the economic needs of all the people.
Your committee further recommends that the convention endorse the following proposals in principle, and urge that same be brought under advisement by the federal and provincial governments and all industrial interests, as well as the proposed economic advisory council.
(a)	That in order to spread available employment in industry, legislation be enacted to shorten hours of labour without reduction of properly established wage schedules, and that an immediate step be taken in this direction by the federal and provincial governments as applicable to all public works and publicly owned transportation systems.
(b)	That piece work and overtime be controlled by government regulation so as to ensure maximum employment.
(c)	That the educational age limit be raised, with adequate and free facilities for vocational training of the youth.
(d)	That a general policy be instituted' as regards old age pensions, superannuation, industrial pensions, et cetera, as may influence the general retirement of workers at the age of 55 years.
(e)	That a rigid enforcement be given the application of minimum wage legislation.
(f)	That sweat-shop conditions be abolished.
It is recommended,
That the federal government be urged to enact legislation during the present session establishing a national scheme of unemployment insurance.
I heartily endorse the report as adopted and commend it to the very careful consideration of the minister and the house.

I should like to discuss one other matter in this connection. The government has recently tabled an order in council dated March 12, 1934, which was passed with a view to instructing the auditor general to begin to audit the accounts of the municipalities and provinces with respect to unemployment relief. The minister will probably remember that at the special session of 1930, speaking on behalf of the opposition, I urged very strongly that the auditor general should be authorized and directed to audit all the accounts that had to do with the expenditure of public moneys for purposes of relief, in so far as they were voted by this parliament. We were told by the Prime Minister at that time that it would be an insult to the provinces to ask the auditor general to do any such thing. I believe he used that word or some word as strong as that; at any rate he used language the equivalent of it. This money we were told was being given to the provinces and they should be permitted to spend it as they thought best. After there has been no end of waste of relief moneys, as the minister well knows, after the sessions of 1930, 1931, 1932 and 1933, we come to the session of 1934, and find that the government has now instructed the auditor general to audit these accounts-to do something which at the present time it is impossible to do. Had such instructions been given at the beginning, had there been inserted in the contracts conditions which would have given the auditor general and his officers power to follow the various commitments and expenditures as they were being made, there might have been something in the nature of an audit. Let me read two clauses from the order in council:
And whereas the audits and investigations which have been made and reported upon by the auditor general, in pursuance of the directions hereinbefore recited, have disclosed the necessity for a more extended audit of the accounts relating to relief expenditures if the interests of the dominion treasury are to be adequately safeguarded; . . . Now therefore His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, is pleased in the exercise of the powers so conferred by the Relief Act, 1933, to order and doth hereby order and direct the auditor general to conduct such audit of provincial and municipal accounts in connection with unemployment relief expenditures as he deems essential to safeguard the interests of the dominion treasury.
There are two questions which I desire to put to the minister in this regard. First of all, this order makes reference to reports that have been made by the auditor general show-

ing the necessity for a more careful and complete audit of the moneys spent on unemployment relief. Will the minister be able to give us these reports? No doubt he has them, because they must be made to him or to the Minister of Finance or to the Prime Minister.

When the provincial conference takes place, would it not be possible for the minister to discuss the whole situation with the provinces to see whether some better terms could not be adopted? Relief Act 1934
with relation to employment are compiled. I noticed, and pointed out to the house, that the figures given by the bureau as to employment may be wholly misleading unless they are carefully analyzed and explained in advance to the public, for the reason that under the head of employment are included those employed by relief moneys as well as those employed by private industry in the ordinary course of business. I think the unemployment problem is sufficiently important to expect the bureau of statistics carefully to distinguish in its statistics on employment between employment that is afforded as a result of money voted out of the taxes of the people for purposes of relief and the employment which arises in the ordinary way from private industry. I would ask the minister if he would take up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is the minister responsible for the bureau of statistics, the importance of having the statistics relating to unemployment make that distinction very clearly in future. I think it is one that ought to be made in regard to all the figures of employment for these years of unemployment, and I wish the minister, as Minister of Labour, would try to secure that information for hon. members of this house. I think it would be extraordinarily helpful in future to find out how much employment has been afforded as a result of moneys voted for relief purposes as distinguished from the employment that has been provided in the last three or four years in the regular course of industry.
While I am speaking on this subject I should like to take this opportunity to say that when I said the figures had been manipulated in a way that caused them to be misleading, I had no intention at all of reflecting on the bureau of statistics or upon any member of the bureau of statistics. What I meant was exactly what the word "manipulate" means. It has a sinister meaning, I know, but it also has the very ordinary meaning of being handled in such a way as to make a certain showing. The figures issued by the bureau of statistics in connection with employment, as they have appeared in the press, would lead the public to believe that the employment afforded by private industry had very considerably increased. As a matter of fact, when one analyses the figures one finds that the greatest increase has come from employment occasioned by the use of relief moneys, has, for example, been in connection with highway construction, most of
which is carried on out of relief moneys, whereas as regards this class of employment the least increase in employment is in connection with the railways, which would be a very good index of the amount of general business going on throughout the country. I want to correct an impression that I was in any way seeking to reflect upon the members of the bureau of statistics. I think that department does its work in a wholly creditable way, but I do think the minister responsible for the bureau, and the Minister of Labour in particular, ought to have seen to it that the bureau of statistics was instructed so to classify the statistics as to make perfectly clear the extent of employment arising out of relief as contrasted with employment in the ordinary course of business.

Very often in this house I have offered one constructive suggestion to the government with regard to unemployment. No progress will be made in relieving unemployment until there is a system, until we have order in the organization of relief. It is an elementary proposition that no one can succeed in any thing without having a plan. One may criticize the Russian plan, one may criticize the Roosevelt plan, but every country has a plan, is doing something. Chancellor Dollfuss in Austria has a plan; the British government have a plan; in the United States they have the National Recovery Act; in Russia they have the five year plan. But here we have a moving picture policy. The only difference between the program of this government and the program at the Capitol or the Regent theatre is that the program at the moving picture theatres changes once a week and that of the government is changing every minute. It reminds me of the story of a woman who was running on the street: someone asked her why she was running so fast, and she said: "I am going to buy a hat before the fashion changes." That reminds one of this government. During the last campaign the poor were given a title-I knew then that the title matter would come before the house-they were called "unemployed." Processions were organized of so-called unemployed, with white buttons in their lapels; they were paid so much per head by the Conservative organization to form huge parades to protest against the Mackenzie King government doing nothing for the

The Prime Minister said, "We must raise our tariff in order to end unemployment." Then he read or told us about promises he had received from manufacturers to the effect that they would not reduce the number of their employees, nor would they reduce salaries. That is what we were told by the Prime Minister, who was very bombastic at the time. Did conditions improve after that special session?
Then -we had the London conference, which had a strong smell of "humbug" about it, and again the tariff was changed. What was the result? We had more unemployment. Later the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General came back to Canada, after the Prime Minister had been given a degree by Mr. Thomas. That wras the first degree he received after coming into office-"humbug." He came back here, at all events, and we had the session of 1931, with still higher tariffs. I remember that my right hon. leader asked the Prime Minister during the session of 1931 if he had not increased half the tariff items, and the Prime Minister said he had not. My leader said, "Let us be fair; let us say one-third," and the Prime Minister agreed to that. Were conditions better after that? They were worse, because the tariff was increased at the request of men who saw only
Relief Act 1934

their immediate profit and who were not sufficiently farsighted to see what were the real interests of the Canadian people.
The argument of the Prime Minister was that by increasing the tariff we would reduce unemployment, and that as a result no man in this country would be in poverty. If his argument had been right we should have had thousands, tens of thousands and millions of immigrants coming to Canada and no one would have been unemployed, because the tariff has been raised again and again. What the Prime Minister said was childish; he was not serious when he said it. He was so far from being serious that he realized that a country is like an individual; it cannot live alone. The Prime Minister said, "Now that we have isolated ourselves we in Canada are like a prisoner within the walls of a gaol. Now we will have to secure outside help." Then he turned to the other dominions and to Great Britain, and we had the Ottawa conference of 1932, with brass bands. What was the result of that conference? We had prognostications about the possibilities, potentialities and probabilities of the hog trade. We had visions of the future as described by the leader of the Conservative party, but that was only humbug, as was his statement in London when he told an audience that Canada was self sufficient. The trade of Great Britain with the British dominions amounts to only nine per cent of the world's trade. These Ottawa agreements were signed at the last minute; the departure of the boat by which Mr. Baldwin travelled back to Great Britain was delayed for one day in order to give him an opportunity to sign these papers, and there was a famous feast at the Chateau Laurier. The newspapers said the tables groaned under the weight of the food and wines placed on them. If my hon. friends think I exaggerate they need only look at the files of the Citizen and Journal in order to verify my statement. It will be remembered that nothing had been signed and in fact nothing had been agreed to up to the very day Mr. Baldwin was to go back. At the last minute something had to be done; some papers had to be signed; some agreements had to be reached. The secretaries and scribes became very busy putting letters and words one after the other, together with rows of figures in order to have something to show the people. That something turned out to be nothing at all. According to the blue-books containing the reports of the Ottawa conference, this was to be the salvation of Canada and was to bring about the restoration of our trade. Is that what has happened?

The conference was such a failure that the government realized that we could not trade only with England and our sister dominions. We are one of the nations of the world; we are proud to be such, and Canada has to trade not only with England and the sister dominions but also with all the other nations of the world. That will be our salvation. When that is brought about we will cease to have unemployment; there will be no need for direct relief for those who have no jobs and those who cannot find a way to earn a livelihood and bring up their families.
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that we will have to pay direct relief until the government comes back to plain common sense. That is all we ask of them. We ask them to lay aside these new programs and plans which are absurd and which destroy the very life of Canadian trade and the confidence of the Canadian people in their own country. Sir, the Ottawa agreements clearly proved that the stand taken by the Prime Minister in London in 1930 was wrong. First he thought he was so great that he alone could dispose of the future of our country. After his experiences with the tariff in 1931 and 1932, he realized that he was wrong. Then we had the conference and agreements of 1932, and after that I hope his ministers were good enough friends of his to tell him he was going in the wrong direction. He saw that the agreements of 1932 were wrong, and then what did he do? He tried to bring about a restoration of the former Canadian trade with all the nations of the world, and with that in mind he and other ministers went to London as the representatives from this great country, While there they met the official representatives of sixty-three other countries, from five continents, three of which the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) has just visited. Yes, five continents were represented at that momentous gathering. The idea of the restoration of world trade for Canada was so important that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) stated in this house that the government was ready to decrease the tariffs and to bring them to a normal level provided other nations were willing to take similar action. He admitted at that time that Canada's tariff was too high. The trip to London was a new experiment; and what were we told by the press while the Prime Minister was in that great city? First of all we were told that the conference was behaving very badly. I do not mean that there was misbehaviour, but that the state of health of the conference was very poor. And then they found a doctor, a political
practitioner who the conference from wreckage, leader of the Conservative party, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada. We learned from the press that two days later the conference was in such good health that it died. It was a marvellous operation which was performed by the Prime Minister.
People do not realize that when power was given to the Prime Minister he received more than that. Actually the Canadian people gave him an axe with which he has completely despoiled Canadian trade. Now he offers a diversion and states, "We have sold so many cans of salmon," when in fact the production of the fisheries has decreased by $21,000,000 when our exports to the British Empire and foreign countries have declined by $11,000,000. At such a time he states, "We are sending so many cans of salmon and so many cans of lobsters." Great! Great! He makes these statements at a time when merchants are selling nothing for weeks and hionths. When a merchant sells a package of chewing gum for five cents he thinks he has made a great profit. The government is acting in the same way.
I want to tell you, sir, that we are sick of humbug; we are sick of smoke screens. We want the truth, and we want it naked, because when an operation has to be made it is not made on a body covered with frills, but on a naked body. If we have to make an operation we must make it on the naked body of Canadian trade, so that we may know the true facts which will enable us to diagnose the sickness. Now, sir, I will diagnose the disease. We hear that in the United States there has been a great improvement in business. Is that improvement due to the N.R.A.?
I will not say that. How is it that confidence has been restored in the United States? I believe the explanation is very simple: The people were fed up with the Hoover regime; they wanted a change, because they had no confidence in the Hoover government. People who had money were not spending it; business was very bad. and the American people were afraid of civil war or revolution. Then what happened? There was a change in government; Mr. Roosevelt was elected, and that very fact restored confidence to the American people. The same must happen in Canada. We have had enough promises; we have had enough experiments; we want a change. We want to open the windows in order to get some fresh air so that we may breathe. It is essential for us to come down to plain facts. In this House of Commons I have

Mr. Chairman, before we conclude the discussion on this resolution I think it is desirable that this House of Commons should recognize the position in which it finds itself in dealing with this greatest and most important of all questions in the country to-day, the problem of unemployment. This afternoon the Prime Minister moved the following resolution which was agreed to:
That when this house adjourns on Wednesday the 28th of March instant, it shall stand adjourned until Monday the 9th of April, 1934.
What does that motion mean as respects the .matters at present under discussion? It means that unless the bill to be founded on this resolution carries between now and Wednesday of next week, so far as any provision on the part of this parliament to deal with the problem of unemployment is concerned, there will when members leave on their Easter vacation be none whatever. I think it is all important that that should be clearly understood. For reasons best known to itself the government this year is adopting the procedure which it adopted in previous sessions of leaving until the very last moment the discussion of the great question of unemployment and unemployment relief. We are within four days of the adjournment of parliament for the Easter recess and within that time we have not only to complete the discussion of this measure but to enact whatever legislation may be necessary to meet the problem of unemployment at the expiration of this fiscal year, which is March 31. Let me make it perfectly clear that if the bill to be founded upon this resolution is not passed before Wednesday-this means not only its passage through this house but its passage through the Senate and its receiving the royal assent by the representative of the crown- there will not be available from the federal treasury a single dollar to assist in the relief of the unemployed. Notwithstanding the fact which the minister has had to admit to-night that the number of families dependent upon relief runs into the thousands and into the hundreds of thousands and notwithstanding there are hundreds of thousands of unemployed, there will not be a single dollar available from the treasury for the purpose of any work of construction to aid and furnish employment to those who are unemployed. More than that, if this legislation is not passed the government will no longer have the power which it has been enjoying when parliament is not in session of making provision by order in council for matters

Relief Act 1934
that pertain to peace, order, and good government and of meeting emergent conditions under that provision.
Further than that, the government will not have at its disposal a blank cheque from which it can draw funds necessary to deal with unemployment relief. It will not have any of the moneys fixed by the legislation of the past year for the purpose of helping to meet the unemployment situation or to relieve rural distress. That is the position; there will be absolutely nothing authorized, nothing out of which the government can make provision to deal with this great question of unemployment relief, and that notwithstanding the fact that the question was regarded by the government, at the time it came into office now nearly four years ago, as so urgent that a special session of parliament had to be called to consider it. We had a special session to deal with the all important question of unemployment relief, which was then declared to be a great national issue; we had that session, a second, third, fourth and now a fifth session; and what is the position at the moment? Should the discussion of this measure, by any chance, last into the middle of next week when parliament adjourns for Easter and the members are away, the government will find itself beginning a new fiscal year without any provision whatever with respect to unemployment in Canada so far as the federal government is concerned. I ask the Minister of Labour and the administration, is it any wonder that unrest and distress are increasing in the country when neglect and indifference to that extent can be shown with regard to the government's attitude towards this great problem? Nothing could be more eloquent of the neglect, or the indifference, or the incapacity-because it is one of the three -of the government to deal with the problem of unemployment relief than this very fact that there will be nothing on the statutes of Canada that will give the government power to turn either to the right or to the left in coping with the problem of unemployment as it exists in Canada to-day unless some legislation is put through before Wednesday of next week. If this parliament should adjourn at Easter without any provision whatever having been made for unemployment, would it be any wonder if a cry of distress went up from one end of the land to the other on the part of the people everywhere who are looking to this federal parliament that has promised to help them in their efforts to cope with the most critical situation with which the country has ever been faced? If we

on this side do not continue, to the extent that we should like, the discussion of some of the matters involved, it is simply because we recognize this fact, that unless some legislation is put through by Wednesday next there will be nothing whatever on the statutes to enable the government to make provision of any kind.
For that reason I say to the minister, I hope he will find it possible to bring down immediately, so that it may be available before the second'reading of the bill, the information which he has promised to-night to let us have. I should like him to bring down first of all the reports of the auditor general to the ministry, or different- members of the ministry, with regard to those cases in which he has discovered that the provision for controlling expenditure, so far as relief is concerned, has been inadequate; next, a statement with respect to the total numbers of unemployed, classified by months and by provinces for the past year-indeed, if he could give it year by year from the time the administration came into office it would be preferable; and the same information with respect to the numbers of persons receiving relief. In addition to that, I wish the minister would also lay on the table a statement giving the latest figures with regard to the total expenditure by years and provinces that has been made under the different relief measures since the administration came into office. If we have this information to-morrow we might let this resolution pass to-night so as to enable the minister to introduce the bill, and we might be able to proceed with the second reading of the bill on Monday, if the government itself is ready to go on at that time. But we ought certainly to have that information before being asked to continue with the measure.
May I add this further word. I hope that between now and Monday the government will consider carefully whether at this session, which may be the last of the present parliament, it should ask this House of Commons again to give it blanket authority to legislate by order in council with respect to any matter it cares to classify under the head of peace, order and good government, and also whether it should ask the House of Commons to endorse a blank cheque with respect to the expenditures the administration may wish to make^ for actual or alleged purposes of relief, especially when the minister has announced, in connection with the work of public construction which the government may bring in, that the government may enter into contracts

I remember when the minister first suggested this plan, which I believe means a great deal to him, I thought he was genuinely enthusiastic about it, but I felt it could not succeed. I cannot see now how putting on the land people many of whom, I suppose, have not had great experience there, can succeed when those who are trained and experienced farmers and who are on property that has been in their family for one, two or three generations are really not self sustaining on the land. I know that in my constituency of Southeast Grey many who are good farmers with mortgages of some

Relief Act 1934
considerable size against their land have lost their property, and many more of them will be in a similar position when the moratorium which at the moment is protecting them is lifted. I should be very happy if the whole farming population in Canada could be made self sustaining, but in my opinion they are not at the present time. At least the farmers in my constituency-and there is nothing peculiar about it-are losing out. If they had money in the bank, that money is gone, or if they had not, they have borrowed just as much as they can, and are not able to pay even the interest on their borrowings. I believe that, generally speaking, is a truthful statement. In endeavouring to carry on, they have sold so much of their live stock that they cannot carry on farming operations as efficiently as they could some years ago.
I do not like to discourage the minister, but I feel this back to the land policy is unsound and will, as time goes on, fail. I do not see how it can do anything else. The minister said that the farmer at least never was out of work. That is quite true. The farmer and the farm woman have more work to do than they should, but they do not get paid for it, and the disequilibrium in population between urban and rural communities arises from the fact, not that there is no work on the farm, but that the people who do this arduous work over years and years, are not paid for it. We all know that, and so to attempt just to take unemployed people, and having given them $600, which I admit is a help, put them on the land and expect that they are going to profit thereby-well, I do not like to say it, but I think it shows the minister knows more about mining than about farming. I believe he is sincere and wants the plan to succeed, but I do not think it can. Some of the older members will recall that in 1922 for ten days there was a debate in the house in which protest was made agaiDst the wholesale immigration that was then taking place; we brought in more and more immigrants and put them on the land, especially in western Canada, and we are producing such quantities of farm products that under the system prevailing markets for them cannot be found. Now we are adopting another land policy. It is not called immigration, but it is possibly the dregs of the former immigration policy; we are attempting to put people back on the land. As the representative of an almost wholly rural community,1 I protest against this; I believe it cannot succeed, and in so far as it does succeed it will make the situation just that much more difficult for the farmers who have been on the land and who
have been trying to farm it for quite some time.
I am not, however, going to say that I think the disequilibrium between the population of rural and urban communities is attributable to just one thing; that is not so. There are many causes, but I am not going to take time to go into them to-night. The tariff has had something to do with it; the money power in the hands of a few people who deliberately built up rapidly the industrial life of Canada has had something to do with it, and an educational system that does not in any way fit people to get the beauty and cultural value out of the country in which they are living also has something to do with it. There are many causes for the conditions as we find them, but as the representative of a fine, intelligent rural constituency I protest against this back to the land policy which is being followed. It may for the moment seem to succeed, but just as soon as these people can get off the land, they will do so. As long as it is the only place where they can have any sort of shelter and can produce some food for themselves, they may stay, but that, after all, is not making a living. Finally they will have to get machinery, clothes and many other things they are not thinking very much about at the moment, and I do not believe they can get them under this scheme. I do not suppose the minister will call this the major policy of the government as regards unemployment, but I think he will find that as time goes on it will fail.

And I believe that under a similar arrangement, namely a contribution of $400, some Men-nonites were settled around Swift Current and some place in the northern part of Saskatchewan. These people had apparently come to anchor around the towns and evinced a desire to get out and get a piece of land and hustle for themselves. There was apparently no municipal responsibility, and a joint contribution was made in a few cases, half by the provincial and half by the federal government.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Suppose a man who is
unemployed in one of these little hamlets in unorganized territory desired to go on the land with his family, is there any way for him to be helped to do so to-day?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I would approve of such
an arrangement. If a person living in unorganized territory, at present on relief or likely to be and without money, wants to take up a piece of land, he would probably be the kind of person who would have a greater chance of becoming self sustaining than even one who had lived in his youth and perhaps beyond youth on a farm and then spent a number of years in the cities. If there were cases of -that kind, and the province viewed it with favour, I would recommend that the federal government join with the province to that extent to settle that man with his family.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
The application will
have to come from the province?

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Under the
Relief Act of 1931 the farmers of Saskatchewan, and I think of other parts of western Canada, were required to give notes for the relief they obtained. Would the minister when the bill comes up give some information in regard to those notes, particularly the amount involved, whether they are being collected, wihat method is being used to collect them, what amount has been collected, and so on?, That has always been rather a sore point with me. It seemed unfair that our farmers should have had to give a note for every little bit of relief they obtained, whereas in the cities it was not so. I am glad the government abandoned that idea.

Limitation of Armaments
There is another thing to which I would draw attention, as there is need of something being done immediately. I am getting letters from farmers in my constituency saying that they must get more feed for their stock, that stock is dying off continually, and that unless they get feed for their horses they will not be in fit condition to put in the crop this spring. They need feed not only for seeding time but in order to get their horses into shape to do the spring work.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
when the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay inquired of the hon. minister what amount was granted to each unemployed per week, in each province, the reply of the hon. minister, if I am not mistaken, was that these figures were not available. As the accounts of each province must be minutely looked into by the minister or his officials, he should be in a position to state whether the treasury is well guarded or the grants made to relieve unemployment were fairly distributed to all the provinces and then to the unemployed. The same applies to rentals. I do not know whether I was well informed, however, I think that in certain provinces rentals are almost entirely paid, while in others no payments are made on them. The distribution of grants to relieve unemployment in the various provinces should be carried out justly, because they all have to pay their quota of taxes to the state. If the government, in the administration of the affairs of the country, acted with reasonable care, its duty would be to scrutinize more closely the statements submitted by the provinces and see that a fairer distribution is carried out.

speechtext: Mr. Taschereau is not responsible for this measure, but the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and those who promised to end unemployment in three weeks must assume such responsibility.

Arising out of an observation made by the minister in connection with this building program, a thought passed through my mind. I was under the impression that the minister had no knowledge as to the extent of the policy, the amount of money that was to be spent or where the buildings
were to be erected. It passed through my mind that a number of sessions ago the government invited the members to let them know of any public works that were required within the confines of their different constituencies. I think that would be a good policy to adopt in connection with the forthcoming building program. I do not believe this should be-and mind you I am not insinuating that it will be-a kind of preelection pork barrel for the party in power. The members themselves have a very clear understanding of the needs of their constituencies in this regard, and I merely make this suggestion in view of the fact that the policy has not been drawn up or agreed upon. I think the government might bear that in mind when bringing the policy to the house for ratification.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Gordon thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 42, respecting relief measures.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
